newsitem.title: USA: Gelatin not free of mad cow disease -- US FDA panel.
newsitem.headline: Gelatin not free of mad cow disease -- US FDA panel.

text.p: A Food and Drug Administration advisory panel said Thursday that given scientific evidence to date, gelatin cannot be safely considered to be free of mad cow disease.
The committee voted 10-to-three to recommend that FDA rescind the exemption gelatin currently has from the agency's regulations on bovine-derived materials.

The panel of physicians, researchers and experts also recommended that the FDA set up a risk-based analysis system and that the USDA establish a more up-to-date method of classifying countries that have a risk of mad cow disease.
Randy Wykoff, FDA associate commissioner for operations, said that the agency would take the panel's advice in deciding what future actions to take.
Mad cow disease -- formally known as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) -- has been found in cows in Britain, France, Switzerland, Ireland and other countries.
Gelatin, used in foods, pharmaceutical capsules, cosmetics, medical devices, vaccines, and candies, is made from the bones and hides of cows and pigs.

The average American consumes about three-tenths of a gram of gelatin each day from such products as ice cream, frozen foods, vitamins, shampoos, vaccines and even surgical sponges, according to FDA scientists.
The committee heard evidence over two days from gelatin manufacturers, who described the high-heat cooking, acid baths and other procedures that they said inactivated the BSE agent.
Experts also said that most gelatin used in the United States comes from either U.S. herds, considered to be free of BSE, or from other nations where the disease has not been reported.
But most panelists said they did not know the whole story.

"I think that after two days of talking. . . (the fact) that there's substantial porosity to our knowledge has become very evident to everybody," said panel chairman Dr. Paul Brown of the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke.
Brown said the panel did not "have enough good information" to answer FDA's questions about how to regulate gelatin manufacturing or the source of raw materials.
But the panel did make its opinion clear on the potential risks to American consumers.

There has not been any definitive link established, but some scientists worry that if humans consume gelatin infected with BSE, they could get a deadly related disease known as Cruetzfeldt-Jakob Disease.
Scientists theorize that a new strain of Cruetzfeldt-Jakob disease that has cropped up across Europe may be linked to eating BSE-infected meat.
"Even though the risk of a single infection is small, the risk to the general population, if we should be wrong, is very, very drastic," said panel member Leon Faitek of San Diego.

Robert Rohwer, a researcher at the Veterans Affairs Medical Center in Baltimore, told the committee that if there is a risk of BSE transmission, it would not be the same for every foodstuff or product that uses gelatin. He said the risk seemed highest for products that are injected or applied to the skin, as opposed to eaten.
